description: Team KhoFra is hunting for Planet X with NASA's SPHEREx data! We're a multilingual Boston team (English, Russian, Spanish, Turkish, Ukrainian, Japanese) building a clear, interactive tool to explore where a hidden planet could be. We're looking for teammates in coding, data analysis & visualization, AI/ML, astrophysics, web development and design/animation. No experience needed, just curiosity and energy for a weekend build. Join us and let's find Planet X together!
summary:
Blink X is a public web tool that lets anyone see how the sky changes in NASA's SPHEREx images. Enter a name or sky coordinates (RA and Dec) and it finds every SPHEREx exposure of that patch, lines the images up, and plays them like a little video: blink, swipe, side by side, difference or time-lapse. It then finds what moved or changed by itself, draws each change as a "Sky Doodle", measures its speed and direction, checks catalogues of known objects, and measures the object's full 0.75–5 micrometre spectrum on the fly. Nothing is called a discovery: an unexplained change is labelled a candidate.

We tested it on the five objects the challenge names. Blink X finds Barnard's Star and Epsilon Indi B moving at their catalogued speeds, sees RW Aurigae grow 59% brighter in a year, and finds WISE 0855, the coldest brown dwarf known, which is too faint for a single exposure: it appears only when the tool adds each visit's exposures together. Its spectrum of Epsilon Indi B shows the water and methane dips of a brown dwarf.

SPHEREx re-photographs the whole sky every six months in 102 infrared colours, far more than any one person can check. Blink X turns that archive into something a student with a phone can search in seconds, the same way Pluto was found in 1930.
details:
What it does. Blink X opens on the real SPHEREx all-sky map with a slider through all 102 wavelengths. Type a name (for example "Barnard's Star") or coordinates, or put them in the URL (?ra=269.446&dec=4.769). Blink X shows every SPHEREx exposure of that spot with its real observation date and wavelength, and five ways to compare them: Blink, Swipe, Side by side, Difference (magenta = new or brighter, green = gone or dimmer) and Time-lapse. You choose the detector band and the field of view (3 to 24 arcminutes). Pixels that NASA's pipeline flagged as bad are repaired from their neighbours and can be shown on request.

Adding exposures together. One selector switches from single exposures to each visit's exposures added up, or all of them. The middle value of every pixel is used, so cosmic-ray hits drop out and the noise falls with the square root of the number of exposures. All five views then work on the deep pictures. An overlay shows the stars of ESA's Gaia catalogue, each moved to where Gaia's measured motion puts it on the date of the picture, with brightness, motion and distance on hover.

Sky Doodles. The backend looks for changes on its own: it finds the sources in every exposure, uses the stars to check the alignment, links moving detections into tracks, and tests steady stars for drift and brightness changes. Each find is drawn as a doodle: arrow (a nearby star drifting), spark (an asteroid), comet tail, pulse (a brightness change) and zigzag (the back-and-forth parallax a very distant planet would show). An Object Card gives the measured motion in arcseconds and SPHEREx pixels, a confidence score, the catalogue check (JPL Horizons, IMCCE SkyBoT, SIMBAD) and a spectrum built from the object's own exposures. Known objects are named; everything else is a candidate, with the reasons it might be nothing.

Spectra on the fly. During one visit a spot of sky crosses all six SPHEREx detectors, so one visit holds its whole 0.75–5.0 micrometre spectrum. One click ("Spectrum of the centre", any mark you place, or the Object Card of a star) reads about a hundred exposures, measures the brightness on the spot in each, and draws the spectrum while you wait, with a plain-language reading and a CSV download. An object that drifts is followed along its drift. A colour band counts as the object's only if a source really sits on its spot there; otherwise the dots are drawn hollow and the text says whose light they are. A star bright enough to overload the detector gets a warning instead of a reading.

Tested on the challenge's five objects. Each is a one-click target, and can be typed as the challenge writes it. What Blink X reports by itself:

  • Barnard's Star: moving 10.0 ± 1.2 arcseconds a year (catalogue: 10.39).
  • Epsilon Indi B: moving 4.6 ± 0.4 arcseconds a year (catalogue: 4.68). Its full spectrum dips at 1.4 and 1.9 micrometres (water vapour) and at 3.3 (methane) and peaks near 4.0: the shape of a brown dwarf.
  • WISE 0855: found only in the added-up visits, moving 8.2 ± 0.6 arcseconds a year (catalogue: 8.15). Its spectrum shows it only from 3.8 to 5.0 micrometres, about 0.6 mJy at 4.5 (WISE measured about 0.45 at 4.6); at shorter wavelengths the light on that spot belongs to a star 6 arcseconds away, and the card says so. ESA's Gaia catalogue does not list it at all.
  • RW Aurigae: 59% brighter in September 2026 than in September 2025, with a brightness chart. Its spectrum keeps rising toward 5 micrometres: the extra infrared of warm dust around a young star.
  • R Draconis: no doodle. The star overloads the detector; Blink X measures changes of 10–20% that it cannot trust, and says so instead of guessing.

Also checked on real data. The detector finds, by itself, the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS moving 175 arcseconds per hour and the asteroids Vesta and Psyche at 37 and 36 arcseconds per hour. The spectrum of 3I/ATLAS is about 65 times brighter at 4.25 micrometres than next to it, which is where carbon dioxide gas glows. Nobody has found a zigzag in SPHEREx data, so that shape is shown on a field that is clearly labelled as simulated. When a catalogue lists a fast-moving object in the field that the search did not find, the page says that too. And an apparent drift that no catalogue names is checked against NASA's WISE (2010) and ESA's Gaia (2016): if a source already sat on that spot then, the doodle is dropped and the page says why.

How it works. The page is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript. A small Python service (FastAPI, Astropy, photutils, NumPy) asks NASA/IPAC's IRSA archive which SPHEREx Level-2 images cover the position, then reads only the bytes it needs from NASA's open copy of the files on AWS: the header, the pixel rows of the cutout, the bad-pixel flags and the wavelength table. It never downloads a whole 62 MB file. Images are put on a common north-up grid and sent to the browser, where all comparing is done. Because it queries the archive live, new SPHEREx releases appear without any change to the tool.

It keeps working when the archive's search is down. IRSA's search service was unreachable for hours during the hackathon. We therefore read where every one of SPHEREx's 101,101 pointings looked straight from NASA's open bucket (one small header read each) and taught the tool the layout of the six detectors. With that record it works out which exposures cover any position without the search service, then confirms each one from its own file. On 38 positions it proposed 99.9% of the 14,635 exposures the archive had listed.

Sharing, embedding and science tools. One short "Sky Code" or link reproduces any view, and coordinates work in the URL. Add embed=1 and only the instrument is shown, sized for an iframe: "Copy embed code" writes that iframe, so any website or class page can show a live Blink X view. Results export as JSON, CSV, SVG or PNG. A Scientist view shows coordinates, wavelengths and signal-to-noise.

Benefits. Students and the public can watch real motion in space within seconds, on a phone. Teachers get the Pluto discovery method with this year's NASA data. Researchers get a quick visual check of any position across SPHEREx epochs, with measurements they can export.

What we hope to achieve. A shared list where volunteers flag candidates for astronomers to review, calibrated (aperture-corrected) spectra, and a WISE overlay next to the Gaia one.

Tools. Python 3.12, FastAPI, Astropy, photutils, NumPy, SciPy, httpx, Pillow, pytest (34 tests); HTML, CSS, JavaScript; Aladin Lite; hosted free on GitHub Pages and Render. The code is open source (MIT licence): https://github.com/Khozhijon/blinkx

Use of AI. The code, the tests, the documents, this text and the slide deck were written with an AI coding assistant (Claude, by Anthropic), working from our requirements. In the final stage, under our general instruction to strengthen the entry, it also proposed and built additions (adding exposures together, the Gaia overlay, the record of SPHEREx pointings, the spectrum on the fly, the embed mode). No image, measurement or date shown in Blink X is AI-generated: every pixel comes from NASA SPHEREx files, and there is no AI model inside the product. The one made-up field is a numerical simulation, labelled "simulated" on screen. AI-assisted commits are marked "Co-Authored-By: Claude" in the git history, and the page says so in its footer and in a metadata tag.

Team KhoFra. Khozhiakbar Khakimov Furkatzhonovich and Francia Constanza Coyotl Cortes.
dataRefs: NASA SPHEREx Level-2 spectral images, Data Release 1 and Quick Release 3 (NASA/JPL-Caltech/IPAC, served by IRSA)
NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA): image search service (Simple Image Access), used to find the exposures that cover a position
SPHEREx on AWS Open Data (bucket nasa-irsa-spherex): partial reads of the image files, and our record of all 101,101 pointings
SPHEREx DR1 all-sky data cube (HiPS, 102 wavelengths) at IRSA: the zoomable sky map on the landing page
IRSA SPHEREx archive documentation: data access
IRSA tutorial "SPHEREx cutouts": used to check our own image reader
NASA JPL Horizons: positions of known asteroids and comets
NASA WISE, AllWISE source catalogue (positions from 2010): check of apparent movers
projectRefs: ESA (European Space Agency) Gaia Data Release 3: star positions, motions and distances for the Gaia overlay and the check of apparent movers
CDS Strasbourg: Sesame name resolver, SIMBAD and VizieR services
SIMBAD astronomical database (names, proper motions, variable-star types), CfA mirror
VizieR catalogue service (serves the Gaia DR3 and AllWISE catalogues)
Aladin Lite v3 (CDS): the sky map viewer on the landing page
IMCCE SkyBoT, Paris Observatory: known asteroids and comets in a field
FastAPI (web framework of the live-search service)
Google Fonts: Instrument Serif, IBM Plex Sans, IBM Plex Mono (open licences)
Claude (Anthropic): AI coding assistant used to write the code, the texts and the slides
GitHub Pages (hosts the page and the slides)
Render (hosts the live-search service, free plan)
Blink X source code (our own repository, MIT licence)
